title: Air pressure, straws & syringes
interaction: A clear box of air particles bounces against its walls and a counter tallies their hits: that tally is the push of the air. Pull the plunger of a syringe standing in a glass of juice and the particles inside spread thinner, fewer hit the juice from above, and the untouched air outside pushes the juice up the tube; suck on a straw and the same happens. Cap the top of a full straw with a finger to hold the juice in, press a suction cup onto a tile, or heat a sealed can and then cool it to crush it.
takeaway: The air pushes on everything all the time; a straw, a syringe and a suction cup work by taking some of that push away on one side.
pitfall: Suction does not pull. Nothing reaches down the straw to lift the drink; the outside air pushes it up because the push inside the straw has been lowered.
why: KS3 physics 'Pressure in fluids' (atmospheric pressure, decreases with increase of height as weight of air above decreases with height) and KS3 chemistry 'The particulate nature of matter' (the states of matter in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page uses pressure as a knob on a phase diagram; this one shows what pressure is (particles hitting a surface) and how a straw, a syringe and a suction cup use it.
needsSource: none; kinetic particle box (elastic collisions give the pressure) coupled to a liquid column whose height balances the pressure difference.

title: Balance & tipping
interaction: Seat children and bags on a seesaw and slide them along the plank until it balances: a heavier child must sit closer to the middle. Stack blocks into a leaning tower, or tilt a bus, a lorry or a tall glass, while a mark shows where the whole thing's weight is centred; the moment that mark passes beyond the base, it tips. Widen the base or move the load lower to make it harder to tip.
takeaway: A thing balances while the centre of its weight sits above its support and tips the moment that centre crosses the edge of the base.
pitfall: The balance point is not the middle of the object but the centre of its weight; and a thing tips not because it leans 'too much' in general, but exactly when its weight's centre moves outside its base.

overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page carries a load to the ground through members in tension and compression; this one has no members, only where the weight is centred over a base, and whether it balances or tips.
needsSource: none; turning effects about the pivot, the centre of mass of a stack, and the tipping condition against the base.

title: Balloons & static electricity
interaction: Rub a balloon against a wool jumper: each stroke moves a few charges from the wool to the balloon, counted on both. Carry the charged balloon toward a head of hair, drawn as strands that swing like tiny pendulums, and the strands rise toward it; the force on each is computed from the charges. Hold it against a wall or over scraps of paper, which have no charge of their own, and watch them shift their charge inside and cling; touch a doorknob to let the charge jump across as a spark.
takeaway: Rubbing moves charge from one thing to another, and a charged balloon pulls on hair, paper and walls that have no charge of their own.
pitfall: Rubbing does not create charge, it moves charge that was already there; and the wall is not charged before the balloon arrives, it is the balloon that rearranges the wall's charge.
why: PhET 'Balloons and Static Electricity' (topics: static electricity, electric charges, electric force) https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/balloons-and-static-electricity ; KS3 physics 'Static electricity' (separation of charges when objects are rubbed together; forces between charged objects) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: electromagnetism: that page shows the field of placed charges and the force on a test charge; this one stays with the balloon and the jumper, rubbing, counting the moved charges and the cling of uncharged things.
needsSource: none; Coulomb forces between point charges, hair strands as pendulums, the wall as a polarisable surface (image charge).

title: Why the sky is blue & sunsets red
interaction: Scrub the Sun across a day's sky: a patch of sky overhead and the Sun's own disc take the colours that come out when sunlight scatters off air along its path, worked out colour by colour from the real sunlight spectrum and shown as screen colours. Thicken the air or add smoke and the sunset deepens to orange and the daytime sky goes paler. Pump the air away altogether and the sky turns black around a white Sun, as on the Moon.
takeaway: Air scatters blue light out of sunlight far more than red, so the sky overhead is blue and the Sun turns red when its light has crossed a lot of air near the horizon.
needs: The ASTM G173-03 sunlight spectrum outside the atmosphere (the 'Etr', AM0 column of ASTMG173.csv from NLR/NREL): the same file solar-cells already builds from, but a different column, since the shipped `spectrum.ts` keeps only the 'Global tilt' column, which is sunlight after passing through the atmosphere and cannot be scattered again; licence recorded as unconfirmed in docs/DATA-SOURCES.md. Plus the CIE 2012 colour-matching functions already shipped by vision-color (`cone-data.ts`, from CVRL; no licence stated at source).
pitfall: The sky is not blue because it reflects the sea, nor because of ozone; and the sky is not violet, although violet scatters even more, because sunlight carries less violet and the eye is less sensitive to it.
why: 'Why is the sky blue?' is the most-googled science question in Glimpse's ranking https://meetglimpse.com/insights/most-searched-questions/ ; Royal Observatory Greenwich explainer on Rayleigh scattering https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/space-astronomy/why-sky-blue
overlapWith: light-optics: that page splits white light with a prism and bends rays; this one scatters it off air, following the Sun through a day, and never bends a ray.
needsSource: Two spectra from one model: the Sun's disc is the top-of-atmosphere sunlight attenuated by Rayleigh scattering (fourth power of wavelength) along the air path for the Sun's height; the sky patch is the light scattered into the line of sight along that path and attenuated on its way to the eye (single scattering), with optional haze of weak colour dependence; both converted to colour with the shipped CMFs. Data: the AM0 'Etr' column of ASTM G173-03 (NLR/NREL ASTMG173.csv; the solar-cells build script reads this file already, licence unconfirmed, cited on the page) and CMFs from vision-color/cone-data.ts (CVRL, no licence stated, credited on the page).

title: Where a bouncing ball's energy goes
interaction: Drop a ball and watch it bounce lower each time while three bars track its energy: height, speed, and the share that has turned into heat and sound; a thermometer on the ball creeps up and each bounce makes a click. Pick a different ball (a basketball, a tennis ball, a super ball, a lump of clay) or a different floor (concrete, carpet, sand) and see how many bounces are left. Drop it from higher and it bounces higher, but never back to where it started.
takeaway: Each bounce turns some of the ball's energy into heat and sound, so it never gets back to the height it fell from.
pitfall: The missing height is not energy that vanished; it is now heat in the ball and the floor and sound in the air. And at the top of a bounce the ball is not 'free of gravity'; it is just momentarily still.

overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page shows kinetic, potential and dissipated bars for a cart on an editable track; this one has no track and one ball, and makes the lost share the point, with the heat and the click to show where it went.
needsSource: none; free fall with a springy, damped contact on the floor (a bounciness setting per ball and floor), the lost energy accounted as heat and sound.

title: Stopping a car: twice the speed, four times the skid
interaction: Drive a car toward a ball that rolls into the road and hit the brake: a strip along the road marks the distance covered while you react and the distance of the braking itself, and the car stops short of the ball or not. Double the speed and the thinking part doubles while the braking part grows four times; make the road wet or icy and the braking part stretches again. The official stopping distances from the Highway Code are drawn alongside for comparison.
takeaway: Stopping takes two distances, one while you think and one while you brake, and doubling the speed doubles the first but quadruples the second.
needs: Typical stopping distances from the UK Highway Code, rule 126 (Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3), as the reference strip.
pitfall: A heavier car does not need a longer braking distance on a dry road: the grip grows with the weight, so the distance depends on speed and surface. Brakes stop the wheels; it is the tyres' grip on the road that stops the car, which is why braking on ice is long however hard you press.
why: The UK Highway Code, rule 126, typical stopping distances, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/general-rules-techniques-and-advice-for-all-drivers-and-riders-103-to-158
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page shows forces changing motion with carts and energy bars; this page is one car, one brake and the two distances every learner driver has to know.

title: Going round a bend: steering and grip
interaction: Turn a car's steering wheel and watch the circle it drives shrink, with the inside front wheel turned more sharply than the outside one so that both roll round the same centre without scrubbing. Then speed up on the same bend: the tyres must push the car sideways harder and harder, until on a wet or icy road they cannot and the car slides straight on; a gauge shows how much of the tyres' grip the bend is using.
takeaway: Going round a bend needs a sideways push from the tyres that grows with speed and with how tight the bend is, and when the road cannot supply it the car goes straight on.
pitfall: Nothing throws a car outward on a bend: the car is trying to go straight and the tyres pull it round. Braking hard mid-corner does not help: grip spent on stopping is grip not available for turning.
why: England KS3 science, forces: 'forces being needed to cause objects to stop or start moving, or to change their speed or direction of motion', https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page changes motion in straight lines and with projectiles; this page is a car's path curving because the tyres push sideways, and the limit of that push.
needsSource: none

title: Tap to pay
interaction: Drag a bank card toward a reader: the reader's coil throws out a pulsing magnetism, the card's own coil, a loop of wire around its edge, catches some of it, and a meter on the card's chip fills as it gets closer. At a few centimetres the meter reaches 'awake' and the chip, which has no battery, switches on and answers by sipping the reader's power in a pattern the reader can feel. Pull back and it falls asleep; slide a metal sheet between and nothing gets through; stack two cards and the reader cannot tell them apart.
takeaway: A contactless card has no battery: the reader's pulsing magnetism powers it through the air for a few centimetres, and the card replies by drinking that power in a pattern.
needsSource: none; coupled coils with coupling falling steeply with distance, a wake-up threshold, and load modulation as the reply.
pitfall: The card is silent until a reader powers it, and the reach is centimetres: it does not broadcast your details across a room. The pulsing field is the same kind as a metal detector's; what differs is a chip that answers.
why: NGSS 3-PS2-3 on electric or magnetic interactions between objects not in contact (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ps2-3-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions); 'Near-field communication' averaged about 18,900 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Near-field_communication/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: metal-detector in this batch: the same coupled coils, but any metal echoes there while here a chip answers on purpose. electromagnetism (level 2) has induction with field lines; this page has only how much power reaches the card against distance.

title: Crashes, seatbelts & the tablecloth trick
interaction: Scrub frame by frame through a toy car hitting a wall with a passenger inside: the car stops, but the passenger carries on at the old speed until something stops them too. Add a seatbelt, then a crumple zone, then an airbag, and watch the passenger's stop stretch over more frames while the force meter on them shrinks. Finally yank a tablecloth from under the plates, slowly and then fast, and see when the plates come along and when they stay.
takeaway: A moving thing keeps moving until a force stops it, and spreading the stop over more time makes the force gentler.
pitfall: Nothing throws the passenger forward in a crash; they simply keep going while the car stops. 'Inertia' is not a force, and a seatbelt does not make the stop smaller, only longer.

title: What a camera's sensor counts
interaction: Open the shutter on a drawn camera pointed at a scene and watch light arrive as specks landing in a grid of tiny buckets, each bucket counting its specks; the picture forms from the counts, and a slider sets how long the shutter stays open. Close it early and the counts are small and uneven, so the picture is dark and grainy; leave it open and the bright buckets overflow to white. Then lift the colour sieve off the grid: each bucket sees only red, green or blue, and the missing two colours of every pixel are guessed from its neighbours.
takeaway: A photo is a grid of counts of light specks, so a short or dark exposure gives a grainy picture, and the sensor is colour-blind: each bucket counts one colour and the camera guesses the rest.
needs: One photograph under CC0 (Wikimedia Commons) as the scene; light specks are drawn at random in proportion to each pixel's brightness.
needsSource: none beyond a CC0 photograph; Poisson counting per photosite, a Bayer mosaic and neighbour-averaging demosaic.
pitfall: More megapixels do not mean a better picture: smaller buckets collect fewer specks and get noisier. The sensor does not see colour, and the graininess at night is the randomness of counting, not a faulty camera.
why: Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Cameras and Lenses' (https://ciechanow.ski/cameras-and-lenses/): photosites counting photons, exposure and the Bayer mosaic; England KS3 physics names 'photosensitive material in the retina and in cameras'.
overlapWith: light-optics (level 1) bends rays through the lens and vision-color (level 1) makes the eye a camera and mixes RGB; this page starts at the sensor, counting, noise and the colour sieve, with the lens taken as given.

title: Straws & suction cups
interaction: Suck on a straw with a slider that thins the air in your mouth and watch the air pressing on the drink push it up the straw, higher the more you thin it; then lengthen the straw until, at about ten metres, no sucking at all can lift the drink any further. Press a suction cup onto a tile, squeeze the air out and hang weights on it until it lets go; poke a pinhole in the straw or the cup and watch both fail.
takeaway: Nothing pulls a drink up a straw: the air pressing down on the drink pushes it up into the space you made, and since air can only push so hard, no one can drink through a straw taller than about ten metres.
pitfall: Suction is not a pull and a vacuum does not suck: the air outside does the pushing, which is why a pinhole, which lets air in, breaks both the straw and the cup.
why: KS3 science, Year 8 pressure in fluids: atmospheric pressure as the weight of the air above (scheme at https://flipeducation.ai/curriculum/gb/science/year-8/pressure-in-fluids); PhET's 'Fluid Pressure and Flow' covers the same ground for older readers (listed at https://elmirador.edu.co/contenidos/phet/en/simulations/category/physics/motion/index.html).
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather: that page uses pressure to drive wind and weather at level 2; here pressure is a push the reader makes with their mouth, and the ten-metre limit is the thing to see.
needsSource: none

title: Why an e-reader looks like paper
interaction: Step into one dot of an e-reader page: a capsule thinner than a hair, full of clear oil with white specks carrying one kind of charge and black specks the other. Apply a push across the capsule and the white specks swim to the top while the black ones sink, push the other way and they swap, turn the push off and they stay where they are. Then turn a page, and only the dots that change get a push while a battery meter barely moves; turn the room light down and the page goes dark like paper, while the phone beside it keeps glowing.
takeaway: An e-reader page is made of specks that are pushed up or down by electricity and then stay put, so it costs power only when the page changes and is read by room light, like paper.

title: Echoes & thunder
interaction: Clap in front of a cliff on a map: a ring of sound spreads out at the speed of sound, hits the cliff, and comes back to the clapper while a stopwatch times the round trip. Drag the cliff further away and the echo arrives later; count the beats. Then start a thunderstorm: the flash is seen at once, the rumble arrives about three seconds later for every kilometre, so counting the seconds tells how far the storm is; a bat and a ship's sonar do the same sum.
takeaway: Sound takes time to travel, so the delay of an echo or of thunder tells you how far away the wall or the storm is.
pitfall: The thunder is not a different event from the lightning; it is the same flash heard late because sound is slow and light is almost instant. An echo keeps the pitch of the original sound.
why: KS3 physics 'Sound waves' (echoes, reflection and absorption of sound; sound needs a medium to travel) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study

title: Falling & parachutes
interaction: Drop a hammer and a feather side by side in air: the feather drifts down long after the hammer has landed. Pump the air out of the chamber and drop them again: they land together, as on the Moon. Then open a parachute under a toy: widen it, or hang a heavier toy from it, and watch the speed climb and then stop climbing at a steady falling speed set by the air pushing back; drop a flat sheet of paper and the same sheet crumpled.
takeaway: Gravity pulls everything down at the same rate; it is the air pushing back that makes light, wide things fall slower.
pitfall: Heavier things do not fall faster in themselves; the feather lags only because of the air. And gravity does not switch off in space or on the Moon; the Moon's hammer and feather fall together, just more slowly.

needsSource: none; weight against air drag growing with speed and area, integrated through time, with an air-off switch; the Apollo 15 drop as the reference demonstration.

title: Fireworks: a bag of sparks thrown in every direction
interaction: Step a firework from the mortar to the sky: the lift charge throws the shell up, the fuse burns as it climbs, and at the top the burst flings the stars out at the same speed in every direction, so they draw a growing sphere that drifts down and slows as the air drags on them. Cut the fuse short or long to burst too low or too high, pack the stars in a ring to get a ring seen edge-on, and pick the metal mixed into the stars to pick the colour.
takeaway: A firework's shape is a sphere because every star leaves the burst at the same speed, and gravity and air then carry the whole sphere down together.

title: Floating, sinking & boats
interaction: Drop objects into a tank (a stone, an apple, a wooden block, a steel ball, a ball of modelling clay) and each sinks or settles where the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; a scale under the tank shows the pushed-aside water. Reshape the clay from a ball into a bowl and the same lump floats; load it with marbles until it goes under. Change the water to salt water or to oil and see who floats now; finally warm the air inside a balloon and watch it rise through the surrounding air the same way.

title: Friction & grip
interaction: Pull a crate across different floors (rubber, wood, ice, oiled steel) with a force meter: the crate stays put until the pull beats the grip, then slides, and a zoomed inset shows the bumps of the two surfaces catching on each other and warming up. Tilt the floor until the crate lets go, and tilt it less on rubber than on ice. Rub two hands together and watch the thermometer climb; put the crate on ice and try to push off and walk.
takeaway: Friction is the grip between two touching surfaces: it holds things still until the push is big enough, and it warms them as they slide.
needs: A few friction coefficients for named surface pairs (handbook values), or surfaces labelled only as grippy or slippery.
pitfall: Do not say ice is slippery because the skater's pressure melts it; at everyday pressures that effect is far too small, and the real reason (a thin water-like layer on the ice's surface, plus heating as it slides) is still being studied. title: Helicopters: a spinning wing
interaction: Spin up a helicopter's rotor and lift off: the blades are wings going round, and the faster they spin or the more they tilt, the harder they throw air down and the more the helicopter is pushed up. Tilt the whole rotor disc to slide forward, backward or sideways; then switch off the tail rotor and watch the body spin the opposite way to the blades, and turn it back on to point where you like.
takeaway: A helicopter rises by throwing air down with wings that go round, moves by tilting the whole rotor, and needs its tail rotor to stop the body spinning the other way.
pitfall: The rotor does not screw into the air like a propeller into wood; it lifts like a wing. Without the tail rotor the helicopter does not simply stop turning: the engine turning the blades one way turns the body the other, and the tail rotor's push is the only thing that cancels it.

title: Hot-air balloons: a bag of lighter air
interaction: Fire the burner under a balloon and watch the air inside warm, spread out and grow lighter than the cold air around it, until the bag, basket and passengers weigh less than the air they push aside and the whole thing lifts. Let it cool and it sinks; pull the vent to drop faster; add passengers and see how much hotter the air must be. Climb high and watch the lift fade as the outside air thins.
takeaway: A hot-air balloon floats because the warm air inside is lighter than the cool air outside, and the burner is the only control a pilot has for up and down.
pitfall: Hot air does not rise because 'heat rises': the warm air is pushed up by the heavier cold air around it, the same reason a cork comes up in water. The balloon is not sealed or pressurised; it is open at the bottom, and warm air spilling out is normal.
why: England KS3 science, the particle model: changes of density with temperature, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ('how do hot air balloons work' is a common search question)
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page heats particles in a box to change state; this page heats air inside a bag and asks only whether the bag is lighter than the air outside it.
needsSource: none (air density from the ideal-gas law and a standard atmosphere)

title: Ice skates: glide forward, grip sideways
interaction: Give a sled one shove on grass, on a wooden floor, on concrete and on ice and count how far it slides on each; ice is in a class of its own. Then put on skates: a blade glides along its length but bites sideways, so pushing off at an angle sends you forward, and leaning onto an edge carves a curve, while a skater who pushes straight back goes nowhere. A zoom shows the thin wet layer on the ice that makes the gliding possible.
takeaway: Skating works because ice is uncommonly slippery along the blade while the blade's edge still grips sideways, and every push is made against that sideways grip.
needs: Measured sliding-friction coefficients for ice, wood, concrete and grass from a cited physics reference (textbook values, no dataset).
pitfall: The blade does not melt the ice by pressure: the melting-point drop under a skater is a few hundredths of a degree. Ice is slippery because its surface carries a thin liquid-like layer and rubbing warms it further, which is why flat shoes slip too.
why: Robert Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today (2005), the standard correction of the pressure-melting story, https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/why-is-ice-slippery
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page treats friction as a slider on a cart; this page is a surface comparison and the odd sideways grip of a blade, and it corrects the pressure-melting story.
needsSource: none (friction coefficients quoted from a cited reference)

title: Keeping things warm (and cold)
interaction: Build a container for hot tea from layers in a palette (paper, metal, foam, wool, an air gap, a vacuum gap, a lid or no lid) and start the clock: a thermometer in the tea and a plot show it cooling toward the room's temperature, fast or slow depending on the walls. Swap the tea for an ice cube and the same walls keep the cold in just as well. Compare a paper cup, a mug, a vacuum flask and a sleeping bag side by side.
takeaway: A good insulator makes no heat of its own; it slows heat on its way out, or in, so the temperature curve bends more slowly.

pitfall: A coat or a blanket does not make warmth and cold is not a substance that gets in; both just slow the heat flowing between the inside and the outside, which is why a vacuum flask keeps iced water cold too.

title: Kites: how a string holds you to the wind
interaction: Fly a kite on a line and change the wind: the kite climbs to the angle where the wind's push, its weight and the pull of the string balance, and a gauge shows the tug in your hand. Move the knot where the string joins the kite to tilt it more or less into the wind, add a tail, and find the settings that make it fly steady, nose over, or refuse to lift; cut the string and it tumbles away downwind.
takeaway: A kite flies because the wind pushes on a tilted surface and the string turns that push into lift, so no wind or no string means no kite.
pitfall: The kite does not rise because the wind blows upward: the wind is level, and the tilt of the kite turns part of its push upward. Running with a kite works only because running makes wind.

title: Magnets & poles
interaction: Drag two bar magnets about on a board: arrows show the pull or push between them, computed from their poles, and a compass needle and a sprinkle of iron filings line up along the field. title: Metal detectors
interaction: Sweep a coil over a beach with coins, a ring, a bottle cap and a stone buried at different depths. The coil's pulsing magnetism is drawn reaching into the sand; when it crosses metal it stirs swirling currents in the metal, and those currents make a magnetic echo the coil hears as a tone. The stone stays silent, the aluminium cap sings though no magnet would stick to it, and the deep coin only whispers; a bigger coil reaches deeper but finds the small things less well.
takeaway: A metal detector's coil makes a changing magnetism that sets up swirling currents in any nearby metal, magnetic or not, and the echo of those currents is what it hears; nearer and bigger metal, louder echo.
needsSource: none; the target is a small conducting loop coupled to the search coil, with an echo that falls off steeply with distance (roughly the sixth power for a small target).

title: Microwave oven
interaction: Switch the oven on and watch the waves from the magnetron bounce off the metal walls and add up into a fixed pattern of hot spots and quiet spots about six centimetres apart. Put in a bar of chocolate with the turntable stopped and see it melt only at the spots, then start the turntable and watch the food sweep through them; thicken the food to see the waves reach only a centimetre or two in, with the middle warming later by conduction.
takeaway: The waves in the box form a fixed pattern of hot and cold spots, so the food has to move through them, and they heat only the outer layer, from which heat spreads inward.

title: Mirror images

title: Noise-cancelling headphones
interaction: An aeroplane rumble reaches a drawn ear as a wave; switch the cancelling on and a tiny microphone on the headphone hears it, the speaker plays the same wave upside down, and the two add to a flat line while a meter shows how much noise is left. Now slide the noise from a low rumble to a high hiss: the headphone's copy arrives a hair late, which hardly matters for slow waves and ruins the cancellation for fast ones, so the meter climbs. Add a sudden clap and watch it get through untouched.
takeaway: Noise-cancelling headphones add a mirror image of the noise so that the two shakes sum to nothing, which works for slow steady rumbles and fails for fast hisses and sudden sounds because the copy arrives a little late.

title: Paper planes: finding the balance point
interaction: Throw a paper plane and watch it glide, rear up and stall, or dive, depending on where its weight sits: slide a paper clip along the nose to move the balance point and throw again, and a trace of each flight builds up. Bend the tail flaps up or down, throw harder or softer, and find the settings that give the longest, smoothest glide; a marker shows the balance point and the wing's centre as they move.
takeaway: A paper plane glides when its weight sits a little ahead of its wings, and a well-trimmed plane recovers from a bad throw by nodding back to the same path.
pitfall: A plane does not fly because air over the top must 'catch up' with air below; the wing pushes air down and the air pushes back. A harder throw does not fix a plane that is out of balance; it only makes it loop or dive sooner.

title: Parachutes: why you stop speeding up
interaction: Jump from a plane and watch the speed dial climb and then stick, as the air's push back grows with speed until it matches your weight; pull the cord and a canopy opens, the push leaps, you slow hard, and the dial settles at a new, gentle speed. Try a bigger and a smaller canopy, a heavier jumper, a stone and a feather, then jump on the Moon where no air pushes back at all.
takeaway: Air pushes back harder the faster you fall, until it matches your weight and the speed stops rising, and a big canopy brings that balance at a slow speed.

title: Pushing a swing
interaction: Give a swing one push and watch it go back and forth at a steady rhythm; lengthen or shorten the ropes, or swap the child for an adult, and see that only the length changes the rhythm. Then tap the push button whenever you like: pushes that land at the same point of each swing make it climb, pushes at the wrong moment bring it down, and a seated rider who leans back and straightens their legs at the right moments climbs with no push at all.
takeaway: A swing's rhythm is set by its length alone, not by how hard it is pushed or who sits on it, and it climbs only when each push or pump adds a little at the same point of every swing.
pitfall: Pushing harder is not what makes a swing go higher, and a heavier child does not swing slower: timing and length are what matter.

title: Pressure cooker
interaction: Heat water in an open pot and watch the thermometer stop at 100 °C as the steam escapes; close the lid with its weighted valve and the trapped steam presses on the water until the valve lifts and hisses, and now the water boils hotter, near 120 °C. Put a potato in and watch it cook in a third of the time; carry the open pot up a mountain to see it boil cooler and cook slower, or choose a heavier valve weight and watch the boiling point climb until the safety valve sets the limit.

title: Roller coasters: where the heavy and floaty moments come from

title: Sailing against the wind
interaction: Turn a sailboat's heading on a pond with the wind blowing from the top and watch where it goes: downwind it is pushed along; across the wind the sail becomes a wing and the keel stops the boat sliding sideways, so it squirts forward like a pip squeezed between finger and thumb; point straight into the wind and the sail flaps and the boat stops. title: Seatbelts & airbags

title: What a smoke alarm senses
interaction: Open a smoke alarm into two little chambers: in the first, a speck of a safe radioactive metal knocks bits of air into charged pieces that drift across a gap and make a tiny steady trickle of current, and in the second a lamp shines across a dark box past a sensor that sees nothing. Blow smoke in: in the first chamber the smoke particles grab the charged bits and the trickle drops, in the second the smoke scatters light onto the sensor, and either sounds the alarm. Slide from the thin smoke of a smouldering sofa to the smoke of a flaming pan and see which chamber reacts first.
takeaway: A smoke alarm does not smell smoke: it either notices that smoke has caught the charged air crossing a gap, or sees light bounced off smoke in a dark box, and the two kinds notice different fires first.

title: Why a spinning top stays up
interaction: Flick a top with a chosen spin and watch it stand; tip it with a nudge and instead of falling over it leans and slowly wobbles round in a circle. As friction slows the spin the wobble widens and quickens, until the top finally topples. Try a gyroscope held by one end and a bicycle wheel held by its axle, run by the same equations.
takeaway: A spinning thing resists being tipped: a push on it turns into a slow sideways wobble, and it falls over only once the spin runs down.
